name: Margaret 'Peg' Tolman
languages: French (the Saint-Pierre waterfront kind, learned buying whisky)
equipment: Leather jacket, a Navy surplus aviator's coat with a sheepskin collar, over a man's wool shirt and dungarees
.45 automatic (Army model, bought off a Portland pawnbroker who asked no questions), 7 in the magazine, in her jacket pocket
Crowbar, two feet of iron she uses to open crates, doors and, once, a Coast Guardsman's opinion

The bill of lading for one crate, 'Church bell, recast, for the Union Church, Carrow Island, Me., Ricker Bell Foundry, East Boston', and the knowledge that sixty quart bottles of Canadian whisky are packed in the straw around it
A letter of introduction to 'G. Coombs, Sculpin Cove', unsigned, in a Portland hand
A set of mechanic's tools in a canvas roll: spark plugs, wrenches, a feeler gauge, wire, tape and a can of oil
A boat compass, a chart of Penobscot Bay with the ledges marked in red pencil, and a waterproof match safe
features: Been Here Before (Survivor origin: advantage on initiative; always knows the nearest way out of the room when a fight or a fright begins; once per long rest, reroll a failed saving throw, fear checks included; the first time each scenario a horror is like the one survived, the GM says one way it is the same). She came through the 1918 influenza and the sinking of a sardine carrier off Pemaquid; the cold sea is her horror

Hard to Kill (Roughneck: once per long rest, when reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, she drops to 1 instead; ignores her first level of exhaustion; advantage on CON saves against exhaustion, cold and hard labor)

Heavy Work (Roughneck: advantage on STR checks to lift, push, pull, break or force something, a door, a barred window, a spiked church door; counts as one size larger for carrying and dragging; carries an unconscious adult at full speed)

Bull-Headed (Roughneck, 2nd level: once per short rest, when she fails a fear check, she gains no Dread but must move toward the source on her next turn and attack it or break what stands between them, or smash something nearby)
Trade: Teamster (Roughneck, 3rd level: advantage on checks to keep a vehicle or boat under way and to get a stalled engine started under pressure)

Grease Under the Nails (Mechanic background: in any harbor she can find work at the boat shed or the garage, mechanics and boatmen talk to her as one of their own, and a few minutes with an engine tells her what is wrong with it without a check, including whether someone made it go wrong)

personality.traits: I laugh loudly and at the wrong times. I am never cold and never seasick and I let people know it. I call everyone 'mister' or 'missus' until I like them, and then I call them something worse.
personality.ideals: The law is whatever a fella in Washington says it is this year. The sea is the sea. A deal is a deal, and I have never once welshed on one, which is more than you can say for the Volstead Act.
personality.bonds: My boat, the Sally Kemp, thirty-eight feet with a Liberty motor, which the Coast Guard seized at Boothbay in August, and which I mean to buy back at auction with this run. My brother Davey, nineteen, who works in a sardine cannery in Eastport and thinks I'm a stenographer. The Portland man who bankrolls me, whom I would not trust with a nickel.
personality.flaws: I have never been afraid of anything and I do not know how to be. When I am, I make jokes, and then I do something stupid. I hid sixty bottles of whisky in a church bell, and I think that is funny, and I am going to find out it is not.

appearance: A sturdy, weather-burnt woman of twenty-nine with cropped black hair under a watch cap, a wide grin with a chipped front tooth, strong scarred hands, a knife scar on one eyebrow and a gold ring in one ear that she says came from a Frenchman. Aviator's coat, dungarees, rubber boots, and a voice that carries across a harbor.
backstory: Peg Tolman was born in a fishing shack at Bremen on the Muscongus shore, the oldest of six, and was hauling her father's traps at twelve and running his boat at sixteen when he lost his leg to a winch. She survived the 1918 influenza, which took her mother and two of her sisters, and the sinking of a sardine carrier off Pemaquid in 1920, which took everyone else aboard. In 1921 a Portland man who liked her nerve offered her a boat with an aircraft engine and fifty dollars a night to bring cases in from Rum Row, and she has been running whisky ever since: Saint-Pierre schooners off Monhegan, cold beaches, fog, Coast Guard patrol boats too slow to catch her. In August the Coast Guard caught her anyway, in the one fog bank that lifted at the wrong moment, and the Sally Kemp is in a government shed at Boothbay with a chain on her. Peg has no boat and owes her backer for the lost cargo. So she is making a run the slow way: sixty bottles of Canadian rye packed in the straw around a recast church bell, consigned to a church, on a federal mail boat, to an island where a man called Galen Coombs will pay $1,800 for it and ask no questions. Who searches a church bell? (Hook: she has met Carrow men on Rum Row. In September, buying cases from the Saint-Pierre schooner Bonne Chance off Little Shag, she saw a Carrow lobsterman she half knew, Clyde something, working on the schooner's deck. She has since heard that a Clyde Tibbetts of Carrow drowned on 2 September. She has not yet put the two together.)
